topics.title: 30.1 Cache hit
topics.summary: A hit occurs when the requested block is present in a usable cache entry. The model can satisfy the access at that level. A hit does not imply zero cost; lookup, data delivery, dependencies, and other execution constraints remain. For writes in a coherent machine, a resident line may still require permission acquisition or coordination. The simple examples in this chapter use reads so that tag residency is sufficient to classify a hit.

topics.title: 30.2 Cache miss
topics.summary: A miss occurs when the consulted cache cannot satisfy the request from a usable resident entry. The system obtains the block from another source, potentially another cache, another core, or memory, depending on the hierarchy and coherence state. The cost is not necessarily a full trip to DRAM. An L1 miss that hits in L2 differs from a last-level miss. State which cache level is being discussed and whether a miss rate is local to that level or relative to all original accesses.

topics.title: 30.3 Hit rate
topics.summary: Hit rate is hits divided by accesses for the stated cache and interval. If 90 of 100 accesses hit, the rate is 90%. A cold-start interval can have a lower rate than steady state even when the repeated workload is unchanged. Aggregate hit rate can conceal expensive phases or uneven requests. A large number of cheap hits does not necessarily compensate for a small number of extremely costly misses on a critical dependency chain.

topics.title: 30.4 Miss rate
topics.summary: Miss rate is misses divided by accesses. In the simple model where each access is exactly one hit or miss, it equals 1 - hit_rate . Multilevel rates require careful denominators: an L2 local miss rate counts misses among requests that reached L2. If L1 misses on 10% of original accesses and L2 misses on 20% of those, then 2% of original accesses miss both levels. Adding 10% and 20% would be the wrong calculation.

topics.title: 30.5 Compulsory misses
topics.summary: A compulsory miss is the first access to a block in a cold-cache reference model. The block has not yet been brought into the cache by a prior access in that model. Larger lines can reduce the number of distinct blocks for a sequential region but can also fetch unused bytes. Prefetching changes when a block is brought in and how demand misses are observed. It does not make data transfer disappear. When classifying misses, state whether the model includes prefetching and what initial cache state is assumed.

topics.title: 30.6 Capacity misses
topics.summary: A capacity miss occurs because the useful working set exceeds the cache’s available storage under the chosen reference model. Even a fully associative cache of the same capacity cannot retain everything needed across the reuse interval. The common three-category classification compares behavior against a fully associative reference cache with a specified replacement policy, often LRU. Classification depends on that reference. It is not a universal label attached permanently to an address.
